$$

Now, since $X∼\text{Bernoulli}(0.5),$ we have

$$
P(X=1)=0.5,\,P(X=0)=0.5,
$$

and since $Y∼\text{Bernoulli}(0.3),$ we have

$$
P(Y=1)=0.3,\,P(Y=0)=0.7.
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}P(X=0\,\cap \,Y=0) & =P(X=0)\cdot P(Y=0) \\  & =0.5\cdot 0.7 \\  & =0.35.\end{aligned}
$$

and since $Y∼\text{Bernoulli}(0.2),$ we have

$$
P(Y=1)=0.2,\,P(Y=0)=0.8.
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}P(X=1\,\cup \,Y=0) & =P(X=1)+P(Y=0)-P(X=1)\cdot P(Y=0) \\  & =0.4+0.8-0.4\cdot 0.8 \\  & =1.2-0.32 \\  & =0.88.\end{aligned}
$$

                    Computing the Probability of an Intersection
canonical_examples.problem: Given that $X\sim \textrm{Bernoulli}(0.7)$ and $Y \sim \textrm{Bernoulli}(0.6)$ are independent, calculate $P(X=1 \, \cap \, Y=1).$
canonical_examples.worked_solution:
Using the multiplication law for independent events, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}P(X=1\,\cap \,Y=1) & =P(X=1)\cdot P(Y=1).\end{aligned}
$$

Now, since $X\sim \textrm{Bernoulli}(0.7),$ we have

$$
P(X=1) = 0.7, \quad P(X=0) = 0.3,
$$

and since $Y \sim \textrm{Bernoulli}(0.6),$ we have

$$
P(Y=1)=0.6, \quad P(Y=0)=0.4.
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}P(X=1\,\cap \,Y=1) & =P(X=1)\cdot P(Y=1) \\  & =0.7\cdot 0.6 \\  & =0.42.\end{aligned}
$$

Example: 
                    Computing the Probability of a Union
canonical_examples.problem: Given that $X\sim \textrm{Bernoulli}(0.3)$ and $Y \sim \textrm{Bernoulli}(0.7)$ are independent, calculate $P(X=0 \, \cup \, Y=0).$
canonical_examples.worked_solution:
By the addition law, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}P(X=0\,\cup \,Y=0) & =P(X=0)+P(Y=0)-P(X=0\,\cap \,Y=0).\end{aligned}
$$

Using the multiplication law for independent events, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}P(X=0\,\cap \,Y=0) & =P(X=0)\cdot P(Y=0).\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}P(X=0\,\cup \,Y=0) & =P(X=0)+P(Y=0)-P(X=0)\cdot P(Y=0).\end{aligned}
$$

Now, since $X\sim \textrm{Bernoulli}(0.3),$ we have

$$
P(X=1) = 0.3, \quad P(X=0) = 0.7,
$$

and since $Y \sim \textrm{Bernoulli}(0.7),$ we have

$$
P(Y=1)=0.7, \quad P(Y=0)=0.3.
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}P(X=0\,\cup \,Y=0) & =P(X=0)+P(Y=0)-P(X=0)\cdot P(Y=0) \\  & =0.7+0.3-0.7\cdot 0.3 \\  & =1-0.21 \\  & =0.79.\end{aligned}
$$

tutorials.name: Introduction
tutorials.problem:
A discrete random variable $X$ follows a **Bernoulli distribution** if it has the following probability mass function:

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/differential/14273447/assets/1dd618fbf1525fa7d7cf21b82517e40f2449a60bf8121eb69bbb6c00b5f0d5ff.svg)

The Bernoulli distribution models the outcome of a **Bernoulli trial**, an experiment with only two events: "success" and "failure".
We label "success" by $X=1$ with a probability of $p$ and "failure" by $X=0$ with a probability of $1-p.$

If a random variable $X$ follows a Bernoulli distribution, we write 

$$
X \sim \text{Bernoulli} (p).
$$

For example, suppose a fair die is rolled. Each roll of the die is a Bernoulli trial. Let's interpret a "success" as the event that we roll a $6.$ Then, the outcome of a roll of the die $X$ can be modeled as a Bernoulli random variable

$$
X \sim \text{Bernoulli} \left(\dfrac16\right).
$$

Therefore, the probability of success ($X=1$) is

$$
\begin{aligned}P(X=1) & =f(1)=\frac{1}{6},\end{aligned}
$$

while the probability of failure ($X=0$) is

$$
\begin{aligned}P(X=0) & =f(0)=1-\frac{1}{6}=\frac{5}{6}.\end{aligned}
$$
